A page of code blocks is a page of grey rectangles.
Which file is which, which one is a shell command and which a configuration file, has to be worked out from the contents.

`code-window` frames each block as a window: a title bar with the filename, traffic lights or title-bar buttons, and, where it helps, a fold.

Every code block on this site is drawn by it, including this one:

```yaml
filters:
  - path: code-window
    at: pre-quarto
```

## Installation

```bash
quarto add {{< var extension.reference >}}
```

This will install the extension under the `_extensions` subdirectory.
If you are using version control, you will want to check in this directory.

Or install it from your editor with [Quarto Wizard](https://m.canouil.dev/quarto-wizard):

::: {.btn-group role="group" aria-label="Quarto Wizard installer options"}

[Visual Studio Code](vscode://mcanouil.quarto-wizard/install?repo={{< var extension.wizard-reference >}}){.btn .btn-outline-primary title="Install {{< var extension.reference >}} in Visual Studio Code using the Quarto Wizard extension."}

## Quick start

```yaml
filters:
  - path: code-window
    at: pre-quarto
```

That is enough: every code block is framed, and its language becomes the filename.

Name the file yourself where the language is not the point:

````markdown
```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
project:
  type: website
```
````

See the [Reference](reference.qmd) for every option, and the [Examples](examples.qmd) for each style and the folding.

## Where it works

HTML formats, and Typst.

Under Typst the chrome is drawn by a wrapper function, and the extension carries hot-fixes for a few Quarto behaviours that Typst output still needs; the [Reference](reference.qmd#hot-fixes) lists them and when they switch themselves off.
